clue.text: 27/22/8's centre of gravity described by German writer?

indicators.note: to describe is to draw round, so the writer's name is drawn round the other letters

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation, placed inside MANN

explanation.surface: A physics question: where does a certain person's centre of gravity lie, as a German writer might put it?
explanation.walkthrough: 27/22 is the cross-reference DOCTOR WHO, and the number after it says which incarnation: the eighth Doctor. That theme runs through every clue that starts 27/22.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul McGann played the eighth Doctor in Doctor Who.

indicators.note: R, right, is sent away from the word
a crackpot is crazy, so the letters go crazy

explanation.surface: A crank is hounding someone until they are worn out, straight away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crackpot' looks like a noun doing the pursuing; it is the instruction to rearrange, and 'pursues' is not a verb here but the letters to work on.
explanation.definitionFit: To use up is to exhaust a supply.

clue.text: A noisy fuss 22 reported in this year

indicators.note: what is reported is heard, so 22 is taken for its sound

blocks.note: 22 down is WHO, said out loud
h.a., hoc anno, Latin for 'in this year'

explanation.surface: A news item about a noisy row this year.
explanation.walkthrough: HA for hoc anno is an old Latin abbreviation found in dictionaries and in crosswords rather than in speech.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal, probably Yiddish-derived word for a commotion: a plain synonym for a noisy fuss.

clue.text: Feature of sailing vessel mother isn't about to accept rising in the morning

indicators.note: the letters of ISNT are moved about
the rearranged letters take in the next piece
in a down clue, rising turns the letters upwards

explanation.surface: A mother refuses to accept that someone is getting up in the morning.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'isn't about to' as 'won't', but 'about' belongs to ISN'T and 'to accept' is its own instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: The mainmast is the principal mast of a sailing ship.

clue.text: Once again drink a toast to theatre over 7D

definitions.text: Once again drink a toast to

explanation.surface: Someone raises another glass to a theatre, toasting its long run.
explanation.walkthrough: To pledge is an old sense of drinking someone's health, so repledge is to toast them again.
explanation.definitionFit: To pledge someone is to drink their health; repledge does it once more.

blocks.note: a town in Greater Manchester, known for its currant cakes
ton is fashion, the fashionable set

explanation.surface: A remark on a Doctor's taste in northern English fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: Greater Manchester is a metropolitan county in north-west England; Eccles is one of its towns. TON for fashion comes from French 'bon ton'.
explanation.definitionFit: Christopher Eccleston played the ninth Doctor in Doctor Who.

blocks.note: the lee is the sheltered side
the initials, first letters, of Director-General, placed inside LEE

explanation.surface: A cosseted Director-General is tied to a strip of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sheltered Director-General' reads as one pampered person; 'sheltered' gives LEE, the side out of the wind.
explanation.definitionFit: A ledge is a narrow strip of shelf or rock jutting out.

indicators.note: half of the word is cut away

blocks.note: b = bowled, the cricket scoring abbreviation
YORKER with its first half, YOR, cut off

explanation.surface: A drunken bowler delivered a yorker, a cricket ball pitched at the batsman's feet.
explanation.walkthrough: Two Doctors share this name, the fourth and the sixth. Half-cut is British slang for drunk, which is the surface's joke about the bowler.
explanation.definitionFit: Tom Baker was the fourth Doctor and Colin Baker the sixth.

blocks.note: Nate Silver, the American statistician and election forecaster

explanation.surface: Silver set beneath gold makes a showy piece of work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Silver' looks like a metal next to gold; it is a surname, and the clue wants its owner's first name, Nate.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word comes from Latin ornare, to adorn.

indicators.note: only some of the word is used

explanation.surface: A grumble that the Doctor's ship has been corrupted a little.
explanation.walkthrough: 27/22 is DOCTOR WHO, so the craft is his time machine, sitting in plain view in the last word.
explanation.definitionFit: The TARDIS is the Doctor's time-travelling ship.

clue.text: 27/22/1's uncontrolled rant in the other place?

indicators.note: the letters of RANT run out of control
the rearranged letters go inside the other place

explanation.surface: The first Doctor lets loose a furious tirade somewhere unmentionable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The other place' is the polite way of avoiding the word hell; at Westminster it also means the other House of Parliament, which is a false trail here.
explanation.definitionFit: William Hartnell played the first Doctor in Doctor Who.

clue.text: Scruffy male's presumably supporting himself outside

indicators.note: the second piece goes outside the first

blocks.note: not kept by anyone else, so he pays his own way

explanation.surface: A scruffy man, apparently getting by on his own and living out of doors.
explanation.walkthrough: UNKEPT is read literally, as someone nobody keeps, and the question mark sense lives in 'presumably'. 'Outside' looks like where he lives; it puts UNKEPT round M.
explanation.definitionFit: Unkempt means untidy, scruffy in appearance.

indicators.note: G, good, is removed: there is no G

explanation.surface: A worthless king's relations.
explanation.walkthrough: G for good is a standard abbreviation, so 'no-good' means drop a G.
explanation.definitionFit: Kin are one's family, one's relatives.

indicators.note: de-tailed: the word loses its tail, its last letter

blocks.note: a groan of complaint, with its last letter cut off

explanation.surface: A former New Zealand athlete lodges a long, itemised grievance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Detailed' reads as 'thorough'; split it as de-tailed. Kiwi means New Zealander, and the runner is a flightless bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The moa was a huge flightless bird of New Zealand, now extinct, that got about on foot.

blocks.note: a cap is a top, a lid

explanation.surface: The twelfth Doctor's favourite cheap supermarket.
explanation.walkthrough: Aldi is a German discount grocery chain common in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter Capaldi played the twelfth Doctor in Doctor Who.

blocks.note: the even letters of iNcArNaTe, the odd ones ignored

explanation.surface: The tenth Doctor, made flesh.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 27/22/10 is the definition, the tenth Doctor; the final 10 does double duty as the start of the wordplay, TEN.
explanation.definitionFit: David Tennant played the tenth Doctor in Doctor Who.

clue.text: Disappear vehicle key in eastern Spain

blocks.note: the Escape key on a keyboard

explanation.surface: A car key goes missing somewhere in the east of Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eastern Spain' is not a region: it is two separate letters, E and E, that hold the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: To evanesce is to fade away, to vanish.

clue.text: Like horseshoes, perhaps, for dead cert at Ascot

definitions.note: 'dead cert' is a noun; nailed-on is the adjective describing one

blocks.note: horseshoes are fixed on with nails

explanation.surface: Horseshoes are a lucky sign for a sure bet at the races.
explanation.walkthrough: Ascot is a famous English racecourse; a dead cert is a horse certain to win, and punters call such a horse nailed on.
explanation.definitionFit: Shoes are nailed on to a horse's hooves, and a nailed-on winner is a certainty.

clue.text: Simpleton to casually improvise on a guitar, say

definitions.text: casually improvise on a guitar, say

blocks.note: an old informal word for a fool, also a pasta strand

blocks.clueFragment: casually improvise on a guitar, say
blocks.note: a musician's word for aimless doodling on an instrument

explanation.surface: A dimwit strums aimlessly on a guitar.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses are informal: an old word for a fool, and a musician's word for doodling on an instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: A noodle is a silly person, and to noodle is to improvise idly.

blocks.note: number one is a nursery word for a wee, urinating

explanation.surface: The third Doctor has a cheeky hit record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saucy number one' looks like a chart-topping song; the number one here is the childish euphemism for a wee.
explanation.definitionFit: Jon Pertwee played the third Doctor in Doctor Who.

clue.text: Man leaving Greek island character there?

indicators.note: the man's name leaves the island's

blocks.note: a man's name, short for Desmond

explanation.surface: A man quits a Greek island, a real character there.
explanation.walkthrough: 'There' points back to Greece: the character is a Greek letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Rho is a letter of the Greek alphabet.

indicators.note: the answer lives inside the next words

explanation.surface: Who on earth lives in a brewery?
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is phrased as a question about brewery tenants; the answer is sitting in plain view.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Who' can mean anyone that, as in 'who dares wins'.

indicators.note: the teacher takes the next letters in

blocks.note: A + VIS, the abbreviation for viscount

explanation.surface: The fifth Doctor's tutor greets an aristocrat.
explanation.walkthrough: A don is a university lecturer, and Vis is the written abbreviation of viscount.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter Davison played the fifth Doctor in Doctor Who.

clue.text: Study of versification's for obnoxious person by the close of Friday

indicators.note: one piece stands beside the next
the close of a day is its end, so only Friday's last letter is taken

blocks.note: sod, British slang for an unpleasant person

explanation.surface: Poetry studies are for an awful person, due by the end of Friday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For' looks like the link to the definition; it is PRO, in favour of.
explanation.definitionFit: The technical name for the study of metre, rhythm and verse forms.

clue.text: Stew recipe? Starter of offal wrapped in a stomach

indicators.note: a starter is what comes first, so only offal's first letter is taken
the letter is wrapped inside the next piece

blocks.note: R, from Latin recipe, the prescription sign
A + GUT; O goes inside, AG(O)UT

explanation.surface: A stew recipe: begin with offal, wrapped in tripe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recipe?' is not a cooking instruction but the Latin word behind the R on a prescription, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A ragout is a seasoned meat and vegetable stew.

indicators.note: to entertain is to take in as a guest

blocks.note: mum as in keeping quiet: sh!

explanation.surface: The eleventh Doctor's mother hosts a visiting American college.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mum' reads as mother; it is the other mum, saying nothing, so SH.
explanation.definitionFit: Matt Smith played the eleventh Doctor in Doctor Who.

indicators.note: in a down clue, turned upside down reads upwards

explanation.surface: Rubbish dumped out, including fish bones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fish bones' reads as one thing; 'bones' alone is the definition, short for sawbones, slang for a doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: Sawbones, or bones, is slang for a doctor, especially a surgeon.

clue.text: Get to know tragic character's destination in the end

indicators.note: only the final letter is used

explanation.surface: Finding out where a tragic figure ends up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the end' sounds like 'eventually'; it takes just the last letter of 'destination'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to find out or come to know a fact.

clue.text: Call to begin party around lunchtime ends in chemical abuse

indicators.note: the party goes round the time
only the ends of the phrase are used

blocks.note: a revel is a party; I goes inside
one o'clock, lunchtime, as the Roman numeral I
the last letters of chemicaL abusE

explanation.surface: Partying through lunch ends in drug abuse, a warning to start again.
explanation.walkthrough: Lunchtime is taken as one o'clock, so it gives I, the numeral one.
explanation.definitionFit: Reveille is the bugle call that wakes soldiers to begin the day.

indicators.note: only the first and last letters

explanation.surface: A gut complaint that ends in a hiccup.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes the hiccup physical; it means a small setback.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal words for a small, temporary malfunction or setback.

indicators.note: only the extremes, the first and last letters

blocks.note: coy is reluctant to give details

explanation.surface: The seventh Doctor is gloomy and shifty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' reads as 'very'; it keeps only the ends of 'melancholic'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sylvester McCoy played the seventh Doctor in Doctor Who.

clue.text: 27/22/2's tenor, feeling unwell, ultimately brought on

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the end letter of 'brought' is taken

explanation.surface: The second Doctor's singer is poorly, which his condition finally brought on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brought on' reads as 'caused'; the words split, with only the last letter of 'brought' used.
explanation.definitionFit: Patrick Troughton played the second Doctor in Doctor Who.
